## Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) {#sec-anova-rcbd}

```{r}
#| label: setup-4-3
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
rb <- read.csv(data_path("pricing_rcbd.csv"))
rb$strategy <- factor(rb$strategy, levels = c("Regular", "Discount", "Bundle"))
rb$province <- factor(rb$province, levels = unique(rb$province))
loans <- read.csv(data_path("loan_rates.csv"))
loans$product <- factor(loans$product, levels = c("Personal", "Car", "Home"))
loans$bank <- factor(loans$bank, levels = unique(loans$bank))
model_rcbd <- aov(sales ~ strategy + province, data = rb)
model_loan <- aov(rate ~ product + bank, data = loans)
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Explain what a block is and why blocking makes a comparison more precise.
2. Describe a randomized complete block design (RCBD).
3. Calculate the RCBD ANOVA table and read `summary(aov(y ~ trt + block))`.
4. Follow a significant result with `TukeyHSD(model, "trt")`.

### Concept

Suppose the retail chain from Section 4.1 has stores in five provinces. Sales in
Chiang Mai are much higher than in Nan, whatever the pricing strategy. In a CRD
this province-to-province variation ends up in the error term, makes MSE large
and hides the differences between strategies.

A **block** is a group of similar experimental units. In a **randomized
complete block design (RCBD)**:

- every treatment appears **once in every block** (the design is "complete");
- within each block, the treatments are assigned to units **at random**.

Here each province is a block: in each province, three stores are randomly
assigned to the three strategies. Comparing strategies **within** each province
removes the province effect, and ANOVA separates the variation into three parts:
treatments, blocks and error.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rcbd
#| fig-cap: "Weekly sales by strategy in each province. Provinces differ a lot, but within every province the Discount strategy sells most."
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(rb, aes(province, sales, group = strategy, shape = strategy, linetype = strategy)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Province (block)", y = "Weekly sales", shape = "Strategy", linetype = "Strategy")
```

### Formulas and Conditions

**Assumptions:** within each block the treatments are assigned at random; the
errors are independent and normal with constant variance; no interaction
between treatments and blocks.

With $t$ treatments, $b$ blocks, $N = tb$, treatment totals $T_i$, block totals
$B_j$ and grand total $G$:

| Quantity | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Correction factor | $\text{CF} = G^2/N$ |
| Total SS | $\text{SST} = \sum y^2 - \text{CF}$ |
| Treatment SS | $\text{SSTr} = \dfrac{\sum T_i^2}{b} - \text{CF}$ |
| Block SS | $\text{SSB} = \dfrac{\sum B_j^2}{t} - \text{CF}$ |
| Error SS | $\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr} - \text{SSB}$ |

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Treatments | $t-1$ | SSTr | MSTr | MSTr/MSE |
| Blocks | $b-1$ | SSB | MSB | MSB/MSE |
| Error | $(t-1)(b-1)$ | SSE | MSE | |
| Total | $tb-1$ | SST | | |

**Test for treatments:** $H_0: \mu_1 = \cdots = \mu_t$. The critical region is
$F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha,\,t-1,\,(t-1)(b-1)}$ (always right-sided). In this
chapter we decide with the p-value: reject $H_0$ if the p-value in the
treatment row is less than $\alpha$. The block row is printed by
R, but our question is about the treatments.

**In R:** `summary(aov(y ~ trt + block))`, then `TukeyHSD(model, "trt")` to
compare the treatments only.

```{r}
#| label: ex-4-3
tt <- nlevels(rb$strategy); bb <- nlevels(rb$province); N <- tt * bb
Ti <- tapply(rb$sales, rb$strategy, sum); Bj <- tapply(rb$sales, rb$province, sum)
G <- sum(rb$sales); Syy <- sum(rb$sales^2)
CF <- round(G^2 / N, 4); SST <- round(Syy - CF, 4)
SSTr <- round(sum(Ti^2) / bb - CF, 4); SSB <- round(sum(Bj^2) / tt - CF, 4)
SSE <- round(SST - SSTr - SSB, 4)
dfE <- (tt - 1) * (bb - 1)
MSTr <- round(SSTr / (tt - 1), 4); MSB <- round(SSB / (bb - 1), 4); MSE <- round(SSE / dfE, 4)
F_tr <- round(MSTr / MSE, 3); F_b <- round(MSB / MSE, 3)
orb <- summary(model_rcbd)[[1]]
tkr <- TukeyHSD(model_rcbd, "strategy")$strategy
ocrd <- summary(aov(sales ~ strategy, data = rb))[[1]]
```

### Example

**Example 4.3.1.** In each of five provinces, three stores are randomly
assigned to the Regular, Discount and Bundle pricing strategies. Weekly sales
(hundred units) are recorded:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rcbd
#| tbl-cap: "Weekly sales (hundred units): strategies (rows) in five provinces (blocks)"
w <- tapply(rb$sales, list(rb$strategy, rb$province), sum)
w <- cbind(w, Total = Ti)
w <- rbind(w, Total = c(Bj, G))
knitr::kable(w)
```

At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean weekly sales differ among the strategies.
If they do, find which strategies differ.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

$t$ = `r tt`, $b$ = `r bb`, $N$ = `r N`, $G$ = `r G`, $\sum y^2$ = `r big(Syy, 0)`.

$$
\text{CF} = \frac{`r G`^2}{`r N`} = `r num(CF)`, \qquad
\text{SST} = `r big(Syy, 0)` - `r num(CF)` = `r num(SST)`
$$
$$
\text{SSTr} = \frac{`r paste0(Ti, "^2", collapse = " + ")`}{`r bb`} - `r num(CF)` = `r num(SSTr)`
$$
$$
\text{SSB} = \frac{`r paste0(Bj, "^2", collapse = " + ")`}{`r tt`} - `r num(CF)` = `r num(SSB)`
$$
$$
\text{SSE} = `r num(SST)` - `r num(SSTr)` - `r num(SSB)` = `r num(SSE)`
$$

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Strategy | `r tt - 1` | `r num(SSTr)` | `r num(MSTr)` | `r fmt(F_tr, 3)` |
| Province | `r bb - 1` | `r num(SSB)` | `r num(MSB)` | `r fmt(F_b, 3)` |
| Error | `r dfE` | `r num(SSE)` | `r num(MSE)` | |
| Total | `r N - 1` | `r num(SST)` | | |

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu_R = \mu_D = \mu_B$ $\quad H_1:$ at least one mean is different

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r num(MSTr)`/`r num(MSE)` = `r fmt(F_tr, 3)`$, df = (`r tt - 1`, `r dfE`)

**Step 4: p-value.** From the R output below, p-value = `r fmt(orb[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)`.

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(orb[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` <
$\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the mean weekly sales are not all
equal across the three pricing strategies at the 0.05 level of significance.

**Which strategies differ?** From `TukeyHSD(model, "strategy")` below:
Discount $-$ Regular (p adj = `r fmt(tkr[1, "p adj"], 4)`) and Bundle $-$ Discount
(p adj = `r fmt(tkr[3, "p adj"], 4)`) are significant; Bundle $-$ Regular
(p adj = `r fmt(tkr[2, "p adj"], 4)`) is not. At the 0.05 level of significance the
Discount strategy has higher mean sales than both the Regular and the Bundle
strategies, and the Regular and Bundle strategies have equal mean sales.
:::

### Reading R Output

```{r}
#| label: r-data-rcbd
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(grp_code("strategy", levels(rb$strategy), each = 5), grp_code("province", levels(rb$province), times = 3), vec_code("sales", rb$sales))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-rcbd
#| echo: !expr show_code
model <- aov(sales ~ strategy + province)
summary(model)
TukeyHSD(model, "strategy")
```

The `strategy` row is the treatment test; the `province` row shows that the
blocks differ a lot, which is why blocking helps.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## What if we ignore the blocks?

Analysing the same data as a CRD, `summary(aov(sales ~ strategy))`, puts the
province variation into the error term:
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-rcbd-as-crd
#| echo: !expr show_code
summary(aov(sales ~ strategy))
```

The treatment SS is the same (`r num(SSTr)`), but the error SS grows from
`r num(SSE)` to `r num(ocrd[2, "Sum Sq"])`, the p-value becomes
`r fmt(ocrd[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` and the difference between the strategies is no
longer detected. The design and the analysis must match.

```{r}
#| label: yt-4-3
ol <- summary(model_loan)[[1]]
tkl <- TukeyHSD(model_loan, "product")$product
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 4.3.1

A regulator records the interest rate (%) of three loan products (Personal,
Car, Home) at six banks. Each bank offers all three products,
so the banks are blocks.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loans
knitr::kable(tapply(loans$rate, list(loans$product, loans$bank), sum))
```

(a) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean interest rates of the three products differ.
(b) If they do, find which products differ.
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-data-loans
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(grp_code("product", levels(loans$product), each = 6), grp_code("bank", levels(loans$bank), times = 3), vec_code("rate", loans$rate))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-4-3
#| echo: !expr show_code
model_loan <- aov(rate ~ product + bank)
summary(model_loan)
TukeyHSD(model_loan, "product")
```

::: {.workspace lines="16"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 4.3.1"}
**(a)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_P = \mu_C = \mu_H \quad H_1:$ at least one mean is different

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(ol[1, "F value"], 3)`$, df = (`r ol[1, "Df"]`, `r ol[3, "Df"]`)

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(ol[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(ol[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject
$H_0$. That is, the mean interest rates are not all equal across the three loan
products at the 0.05 level of significance.

**(b)** Car $-$ Personal (p adj = `r fmt(tkl[1, "p adj"], 4)`) and Home $-$ Personal
(p adj = `r fmt(tkl[2, "p adj"], 4)`) are significant; Home $-$ Car
(p adj = `r fmt(tkl[3, "p adj"], 4)`) is not. At the 0.05 level of significance,
personal loans have a higher mean interest rate than car loans and home loans,
and car and home loans have equal mean rates.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Sums of squares | $\text{SSTr} = \sum T_i^2/b - \text{CF}$; $\text{SSB} = \sum B_j^2/t - \text{CF}$; $\text{SSE} = \text{SST} - \text{SSTr} - \text{SSB}$ |
| df | treatments $t-1$; blocks $b-1$; error $(t-1)(b-1)$; total $tb-1$ |
| Test for treatments | $F_{\text{cal}} = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$, df $= (t-1,\ (t-1)(b-1))$; reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$ |
| R | `summary(aov(y ~ trt + block))`; `TukeyHSD(model, "trt")` |

### Exercises

**4.3.1** For each study, say whether it is a CRD or an RCBD, and name the
treatments and (if any) the blocks.

(a) Twenty shops are randomly assigned to four store layouts, five shops each.
(b) Four store layouts are each tried once in each of five shopping malls, with the layout randomly assigned to shops within each mall.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 4.3.1"}
(a) CRD; treatments: the four layouts; no blocks.
(b) RCBD; treatments: the four layouts; blocks: the five malls.
:::

**4.3.2** An RCBD has 4 treatments and 6 blocks, with SST = 120, SSTr = 36 and
SSB = 54. Complete the ANOVA table. The p-value for treatments is
`r fmt(pf(6, 3, 15, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)`; test the treatments at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 4.3.2"}
SSE = 120 $-$ 36 $-$ 54 = 30; df: treatments 3, blocks 5, error 15, total 23.
MSTr = 36/3 = 12, MSB = 54/5 = 10.8, MSE = 30/15 = 2.
$F_{\text{cal}}$ = 12/2 = 6.000 for treatments.
p-value = `r fmt(pf(6, 3, 15, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject
$H_0$. That is, the treatment means are not all equal at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::
